title: Chapter 1: Introduction: The Nature of Drugs & Drug Development & Regulation
authors: Todd W. Vanderah; Bertram G. Katzung
file: Chapter 1_ Introduction_ The Nature of Drugs -amp;amp; Drug Development -amp;amp; Regulation.pdf
about: Pharmacology can be defined as the study of substances that interact with living systems through chemical processes. In the most general sense, a drug may be defined as any substance that brings about a change in biologic function through its chemical actions. In most cases, the drug molecule interacts as an agonist (activator) or antagonist (inhibitor) with a specific target molecule that plays a regulatory role in the biologic system. This target molecule is called a receptor.
sections: General Principles of Pharmacology: The Nature of Drugs (physical nature, size, shape, rational drug design, receptor nomenclature)
Pharmacokinetic Principles (permeation, Fick's law, ionization of weak acids and bases)
Drug Development & Regulation (discovery, preclinical safety, evaluation in humans, FDA, IND & NDA, orphan drugs)
read_for: 'Drug-Body Interactions' and Figure 1-1: pharmacodynamics (drug on body) vs pharmacokinetics (body on drug), the 9/22 framing.
'Pharmacodynamic Principles' A: agonist, pharmacologic antagonist, allosteric enhancement/inhibition (Figure 1-2 dose-response panels A-D).
'Pharmacodynamic Principles' C and Figure 1-3: the Ri/Ra two-state model; full agonist, partial agonist (intrinsic efficacy), neutral antagonist, inverse agonist, constitutive activity.
'Pharmacodynamic Principles' B: agonists that act by inhibiting breakdown of the endogenous ligand (cholinesterase inhibitors), a preview of the autonomic block.
'Pharmacodynamic Principles' D and E: duration of action (covalent binding, desensitization) and receptors vs inert binding sites (albumin).
'The Nature of Drugs': drug, receptor, xenobiotic, poison, toxin, chemical antagonist, 'the dose makes the poison'.
'Drug Size' and 'Drug Shape' (Table 1-2, carvedilol enantiomers): why MW 100-1000 and chirality matter for receptor fit.
beyond_lecture: Part II (Drug Development & Regulation): screening, preclinical safety tests (Table 1-5), phases of clinical trials, IND/NDA, FDA legislation (Table 1-6), orphan drugs.
Pharmacokinetic Principles: permeation, Fick's law, ionization and pH trapping (Table 1-4), transporters (Table 1-3) - Exam 2 territory for a PK course, not Gottlieb's lectures.
History of pharmacology and large-molecule approval trends (Table 1-1).
Drug Groups and Sources of Information.

terms.chapter_definition: the study of substances that interact with living systems through chemical processes.
any substance that brings about a change in biologic function through its chemical actions.
a specific target molecule that plays a regulatory role in the biologic system, with which the drug interacts as an agonist (activator) or antagonist (inhibitor).
the actions of the drug on the body.
the actions of the body on the drug; they govern the absorption, distribution, and elimination of drugs.
effect produced by the receptor pool in the Ra form in the absence of agonist.
agonist drugs that, at concentrations sufficient to saturate the receptor pool, activate their receptor-effector systems to the maximum extent of which the system is capable.
drugs that bind to the same receptors and activate them in the same way but do not evoke as great a response, no matter how high the concentration; said to have low intrinsic efficacy.
a drug with much stronger affinity for the Ri than the Ra state that reduces any constitutive activity, resulting in effects opposite to those of conventional agonists.
a nonregulatory molecule such as plasma albumin whose binding of a drug results in no detectable change in the function of the biologic system.
